title: Exit, Voice, and Nikole Hannah-Jones
author: Ilya Somin
summary: Ilya Somin reads Nikole Hannah-Jones's essay as a testament to the value of exit rights and school choice, even though she does not draw that lesson herself. He connects her original decision to Albert Hirschman's argument that exit can harm institutions that savvy members might otherwise reform through voice. Drawing on his book Free to Move, Somin explains that Hirschman's case holds only in narrow conditions, and that peer-reviewed voucher studies show public schools left behind actually improve. He argues that the core problem at schools like P.S. 307 is not money or activism but poor incentives, since staff are paid the same regardless of results. Somin adds personal testimony about exit rights, from his family's emigration from the Soviet Union and later move to Lexington for better schools, to the METCO program he saw in high school and his daughter's pandemic-era move to a private school, where she eventually learned to read through sight-word memorization.
points: Somin credits Hannah-Jones for publicly acknowledging error on an issue close to her ideological commitments.
Hirschman's voice-over-exit argument requires conditions that rarely hold, he argues, including that exiting parents could have forced reforms.
Voucher research finds that public schools facing exit improve, while added funding alone shows little benefit.
Schools with ample funding fail when employees face no incentive tied to student outcomes.
Somin also urges ending exclusionary zoning and adopting universal school choice to break the link between residence and schooling.
quotes: Hannah-Jones' story is a testament to the value of exit rights and choice. Although she does not seem to recognize it, the best way to help students from less advantaged families than her own is to expand exit and choice opportunities for them.
While I think Hannah-Jones hasn't fully drawn the right lessons from her experience, I commend her for her willingness to acknowledge error.
Peer-reviewed studies of the effects of vouchers find that they actually improve the quality of public schools "left behind" by those who exit.
More fundamentally, the main problems besetting those schools are not lack of resources or lack of activism, but poor incentives.
The problem is that school officials and employees have little incentive to use those resources in ways that actually facilitate quality education.
The episode shows that even high-quality schools and teachers cannot fully substitute for parental judgment of their kids' specific needs.
In sum, no school is perfect, and parents need to be attentive to their kids' individual situations.
